title: Operating Systems
body:
COMP 3659 covers the layer between programs and hardware. An operating system exists because a
machine has one processor, one memory and one disk, and several programs want all three at
once. It decides which program runs next, gives each one an address space that appears private
and larger than the installed memory, keeps concurrent programs from corrupting each other's
data, and turns a disk of numbered blocks into files with names.

The course is organised around [[Synchronization]]. Most of the material builds toward one
problem: two things running at the same time and touching the same data produce a result that
depends on the exact interleaving, which changes between runs. That is the point where a
program can be correct every time it is tested and wrong in production, so correctness stops
being observable and starts requiring proof.

It sits directly on [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]], reusing its interrupts, I/O and context
switching, and it builds the kernel out of the structures from [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]].

## Topics

### The kernel and the two modes

The processor has two modes. In user mode certain instructions are illegal, including the ones
that touch device registers and change the memory map. In supervisor mode everything is legal.
Application code runs in the first, the [[Kernel]] runs in the second, and the boundary is what
makes protection possible: a program cannot reach another program's memory because the
instructions that would let it are unavailable.

A [[System Call]] is the doorway between them. The program places a request in an agreed place
and executes an instruction that switches to supervisor mode and jumps into the kernel, which
performs the operation and switches back. Reading a file is a system call, and so is asking for
memory, because both require privilege the program lacks.

```
user mode      program runs, calls read()
                     |  traps into the kernel
supervisor     kernel validates the arguments, talks to the disk
                     |  returns
user mode      program continues with the data
```

[[Operating System Structure]] covers how the kernel itself is divided, which is a
[[Complexity]] decision of the kind [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] describes, applied
to the largest program on the machine. [[Supervisor State]] is the mode bit in the processor,
already met in [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]].

### Processes

A process is a program in execution, with its own address space, its own open files and its own
place in the instruction stream. Two copies of the same program running at once are two
processes with the same code and separate everything else.

The kernel tracks each one in a [[PCB]], a process control block, which is a [[Control Block]]
holding the saved registers, the program counter, the memory map and the open file table. When
the kernel takes the processor away from a process, everything needed to resume it goes into
the PCB, and restoring from there is what makes the interruption invisible. PCBs are usually
chained into a doubly [[Linked List]].

[[Process State]] moves a process between three conditions, and the transitions are what the
kernel manages:

```
              scheduled
   ready  ──────────────>  running
     ^                        |
     |  I/O completes         |  requests I/O, or blocks
     |                        v
     └────────────────────  waiting
```

Every process sits in a [[Queue]] while it is neither running nor finished. It waits in the
[[Ready Queue]] while it is runnable, and moves to a [[Wait Queue]], which is [[FIFO]], when it
enters a [[Waiting state]] until whatever it waits for arrives. [[Process Priority]] influences
which ready process is chosen, and [[Processes]] covers the lifecycle in full.

### Threads

A [[Thread]] is one flow of execution inside a process. Threads in one process share the
address space, so they share every global variable and every heap allocation, and each has its
own stack and its own registers.

That sharing is what makes threads cheap to switch between and dangerous to write. Two
processes cannot corrupt each other's variables, because the hardware refuses. Two threads
share the variables by design, which is the whole point and the whole problem.

### Scheduling

[[CPU Scheduling]] decides which ready thread runs next. The policies trade against each other:
running short jobs first raises throughput and the number of finished jobs, while a stream of
short jobs can leave a long one waiting indefinitely, which is [[Starvation]]. [[Fairness]] is
the property that prevents it, usually by raising the priority of anything that has waited a
long time.

[[Processor Affinity]] is a thread's preference for the core it ran on last, because a thread
moved to another core arrives at a [[Cache]] holding none of its data and runs slowly until the
cache refills.

[[Amdahl's Law]] caps what more cores can achieve. If a fraction $s$ of a program has to run
serially, the speedup on $n$ cores is at most $1 / (s + (1-s)/n)$, so a program that is 10%
serial cannot exceed a speedup of 10 no matter how many cores it gets. That serial fraction is
the [[Critical Section]] defined next, which is what connects the scheduling half of the course
to the synchronisation half.

### Why concurrency breaks things

[[Concurrency]] means two threads making progress over the same period. The problem is that a
statement in a high-level language is several instructions, and a thread can be interrupted
between any two of them.

```
counter++     compiles to three instructions:
                  load  counter -> register
                  add   1
                  store register -> counter
```

Two threads each running `counter++` once, on a counter starting at 5, can interleave like
this:

```
T1: load  (reads 5)
T2: load  (reads 5)          <- T2 read before T1 wrote
T1: add, store (writes 6)
T2: add, store (writes 6)    <- overwrites, the increment is lost
counter is 6, and it should be 7
```

Nothing is wrong with either thread. The bug lives in the interleaving, it appears on some runs
and not others, and adding a print statement changes the timing enough to hide it. That is a
race condition, and it is why this course exists.

A [[Critical Section]] is the code performing a transaction on shared data, `counter++` above.
It has to be serialised, meaning at most one thread executes it at a time. The surrounding code
has four parts: the entry section that acquires the right to proceed, the critical section, the
exit section that releases it, and the remainder section.

### What a correct solution has to do

Three requirements together, and dropping any one produces a solution that fails in a specific
way.

[[Mutual Exclusion]] allows at most one thread inside the critical section, which is the point
of the exercise. [[Progress]] requires that when no thread is inside, the decision about who
enters next is made only by the threads currently trying, so a thread doing something unrelated
cannot block the entrance. [[Bounded Waiting]] puts an upper limit on how many times other
threads can enter ahead of a waiting one, which is what prevents starvation.

### Four ways to enforce it

| Approach | Mechanism | Limitation |
|---|---|---|
| [[Peterson's Solution]] | software alone, using a `flag` array and a `turn` variable | busy-waits, covers two processes, and breaks if the compiler or processor reorders the two assignments |
| [[TAS]] | an atomic test-and-set instruction | requires [[Hardware]] support and still busy-waits, giving a [[Spin Lock]] |
| [[Locks]] and [[Mutex Lock]] | acquire, run the critical section, release | blocking, and coarse if one lock covers too much |
| [[Semaphores]] | a non-negative counter with a [[Wait Queue]] | general and correct, and easy to misuse |

[[Peterson's Solution]] shows that the problem is solvable with ordinary reads and writes, and
its fragility shows why nobody does it that way. The two assignments in its entry section have
to happen in that order, and a compiler that reorders them for speed breaks the algorithm
silently.

Hardware support fixes that with one instruction that reads a value and writes a new one with
nothing able to intervene. [[TAS]] is that instruction, and a lock built from it spins in a
loop until it succeeds. A [[Spin Lock]] holds the processor while waiting, which is the right
choice when the expected wait is shorter than a context switch and wasteful otherwise.

A [[Semaphores|semaphore]] gives up the processor while it waits. It is a counter with two
operations:
acquiring decrements it, and a thread that finds it at zero goes into a [[Waiting state]] on the
semaphore's queue. Releasing increments the counter and wakes a waiting thread. A
[[Mutex Lock]] is a semaphore whose counter only ever holds 0 or 1. [[POSIX]] exposes this as
`sem_init`, `sem_wait`, which blocks at zero, and `sem_post`, which is called on leaving the
critical section.

```c
sem_wait(&mutex);        // enter: blocks if another thread is inside
counter++;               // critical section
sem_post(&mutex);        // exit: releases, and wakes a waiting thread
```

### The bounded buffer

The [[Bounded Buffer Problem]] is the standard exercise and the one worth working through,
because it needs all three semaphores for three different reasons. A producer thread adds items
to a fixed-length buffer and a [[Producer Consumer|consumer]] thread removes them.

```
mutex       initialised to 1    protects the buffer itself from two threads at once
slot_avail  initialised to n    counts free slots, so the producer sleeps when full
item_avail  initialised to 0    counts stored items, so the consumer sleeps when empty
```

```c
// producer                       // consumer
sem_wait(&slot_avail);            sem_wait(&item_avail);
sem_wait(&mutex);                 sem_wait(&mutex);
   insert(item);                     item = remove();
sem_post(&mutex);                 sem_post(&mutex);
sem_post(&item_avail);            sem_post(&slot_avail);
```

The two counting semaphores handle waiting for space and waiting for data, and the mutex
handles the buffer itself. Acquiring them in the wrong order deadlocks: a producer holding the
mutex and then waiting for a free slot blocks the consumer that would have freed one.

### Communicating between processes

Threads share memory by default and processes do not, so processes need a mechanism.
[[Inter-process Communication]] offers two, with opposite trade-offs.

[[Shared Memory]] maps one region into several address spaces, so a write by one process is
immediately visible to the others at full memory speed, and every synchronisation problem above
is left to the processes involved. [[Message Passing]] sends data through the kernel, which
copies it and handles the coordination, so it is slower and correct by construction.
[[Piping]] is the shell-level form of message passing, connecting one program's output to
another's input, covered in [[Shell]]. [[Process Communication]] covers the general topic.

### Memory

[[Virtual Memory]] gives each process an [[Address Space]] that looks private and contiguous.
Every address the program uses is virtual, and hardware translates it to a physical address in
[[Main memory]] on every access, using tables the kernel maintains.

That indirection buys three things at once. Processes are isolated, because a process has no
way to name another process's memory. Programs can be written without knowing where they will
be loaded. The total memory in use can exceed what is installed, because a page not currently
needed can be written to disk and its physical frame reused, then fetched back when it is
touched. [[Memory Mapping]] covers the translation. First year gives the layout inside one
address space in [[Stack and Heap]], [[Static Allocation]] and [[Dynamic Allocation]].

### Files and storage

A disk stores numbered blocks and knows nothing about names or folders. [[File Systems]] is the
layer that turns those blocks into a tree of named files, and it separates two things. The
[[File System Interface]] is what a program uses, meaning open, read, write and seek on a
[[File]] inside a [[Directory]]. [[Mass Storage Structure]] is how those bytes are laid out on
the device and how simultaneous requests to it are ordered, which matters because a mechanical
disk spends most of its time moving the head.

[[Buffering]] and [[Double Buffering]] carry over from [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] for the same
reason they existed there, which is a speed mismatch between a device and the program reading
from it.

## Related courses

- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] (COMP 2659) is the hardware this course runs on, supplying
  [[Interrupts]], [[Context Switching]], [[Direct Memory Access]], [[Polling]],
  [[Vector Tables]] and the first appearance of [[Concurrency]].
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] (COMP 2655) supplies [[CPU]], [[Cache]], [[Kernel]],
  [[System Call]] and [[Main memory]].
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] (COMP 2631) supplies the [[Queue]], [[Linked List]], [[Stack]]
  and [[Heap]] the kernel is built from.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] (COMP 1633) supplies [[Memory]],
  [[Stack and Heap]] and [[Address]].
- [[PROGRAMMING PARADIGMS]] (COMP 3649) makes the opposite argument about shared state, since
  a race needs a writer and [[Immutability]] removes it.
- [[WEB DEVELOPMENT FOR CS]] (COMP 3612) repeats the blocking argument one layer up, where
  [[Node.js]] serves many requests from one thread and a thread-per-request server parks one
  thread each.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] treats scheduling as algorithm design, and [[Amdahl's Law]] as
  a complexity statement about parallelism.
